definition: Desecrate means to violate the sacredness of a thing or place.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word desecrate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know desecrate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The trail gate closes at dusk less for safety than to keep photographers from desecrating the cliff paintings with flash rigs and fingerprints.
Disturb only jostles a place — noise in the reading room, footprints on raked gravel; an apology mends it, where desecrate wounds a place's holiness past any apology's reach.
Damage goes further than disturb — something breaks and stays broken; desecrate claims the most: the harm lands on a place's holiness, an injury no repair crew can reach.

To violate is to break in on whatever is protected — a law, a border, a trust, a quiet space. Desecrate is the special case where the protected thing is sacred: the act insults the holiness itself, not just the rule around it.

To dishonor is to strip the respect from a person or a memory — a family name, a veteran, a promise. Desecrate needs a sacred thing or place for its target — an altar, a grave, a scripture — and the insult lands on its holiness.

When the army wintered in the captured city in 1644, it quartered its horses in the cathedral: hay heaped where the choir had sung, dung on the tomb slabs, muskets stacked against the font.
The troopers called it convenience; their colonel meant it as a message, and both sides' chroniclers agreed the army had desecrated the place.
The pews they burned that winter were furniture — the building was an altar, and everyone understood which loss was the wound.
Desecrate is the exact word for that winter, because it means to violate the sacredness of a thing or place — the target must be holy to someone, and the act insults exactly that.
Vandalism breaks property; desecration breaks a promise a community made about what would be kept apart and honored.
Desecrate is the strongest accusation in this unit, and it needs a sacred object to land on: graves, altars, memorials, scripture.
For everyday property, vandalize; for a surface's looks, this unit's deface; for purity more broadly — a spring, a snowfield — defile.
Call a parking violation desecration and you have spent the word.

The spring above Calder's Ford has been a shrine for as long as the town has records: ribbons on the hawthorn, coins in the pool, weddings blessed at the waterline every June.
So when the resort's contractors rerouted the spring into a concrete channel and poured a patio slab over the pool, the town did not talk about property lines.
At the hearing, the word people kept reaching for was desecrate.
The company had permits; nothing it did was against code.
But the harm, speakers said, was not to any rule — it was to the holiness of the place itself, and no fine or replanting could give that back.
The county's settlement was strange and telling: money for the town, yes, but also a public apology read aloud at the water — which everyone present knew could not undo what had been done.
